Photo by Guillaume DECAMME / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Russian airports entered a third consecutive night of disruption early Friday, Sept. 4, as another wave of drones approached Moscow following widespread cancellations, delays and rolling flight restrictions a day earlier. Saratov’s Gagarin Airport also imposed fresh restrictions early Friday, extending the disruption beyond Moscow. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . The latest wave marks mounting pressure on Russia’s aviation system following President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Sept. 1 warning that Russian airspace would increasingly become unsafe as Ukraine expands long-range drone operations. On Sept. 2, Flightradar24 recorded 21 cancellations and 235 delays at Sheremetyevo, while Vnukovo registered 22 cancellations and 94 delays – a combined 43 cancellations and 329 delays. Advertisement At least 27 foreign flights to and from Moscow were also canceled, affecting carriers including Pegasus Airlines, Turkish Airlines and flydubai. By Sept. 2 into Sept. 3, restrictions widened to all four Moscow airports – Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, Domodedovo and Zhukovsky – as well as airports in Sochi, Gelendzhik, Penza, Saratov, Yaroslavl and Nizhny Novgorod. More than 120 flights were disrupted at Sheremetyevo and Vnukovo alone. Sobyanin said 548 drones flew toward the Moscow region between the morning of Sept. 2 and noon Sept. 3, with 143 intercepted on approaches to the capital. The disruption also forced Moscow-bound aircraft to divert. St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport received several flights originally headed for Moscow, while Nizhny Novgorod took in 16. Other Topics of Interest Russian Strike on Odesa Kills 1, Injures at Least 3 The deadly attack came a day after another Russian strike wounded 17 people in the Black Sea port city. Flightradar24 data cited by RFE/RL showed four Russian airports among the world’s five most disrupted airports on Thursday. Ukrainian aviation expert Valeriy Romanenko told RFE/RL that Kyiv may be seeking sustained pressure rather than temporary closures. “The strategy is to make these airports unusable,” he said, arguing that repeated drone attacks could force Russia to divert significant air-defense resources to protect major aviation hubs. Advertisement Alexander Lanetsky, CEO of Lithuania-based aircraft brokerage Friendly Avia Support, told Current Time that prolonged disruption in Moscow could reverberate across Russia because of the country’s vast territory and dependence on domestic aviation. Foreign carriers also face growing pressure. Turkey, Uzbekistan, the UAE, China and Egypt account for about 72% of Russia’s international passenger traffic. Moscow has sought to reassure airlines, with Russia’s Transport Ministry saying Thursday that it provided foreign carriers with additional explanations about airport and airspace safety. Rosaviatsiya maintained that Russian aviation infrastructure continued operating normally, even as repeated restrictions, cancellations and diversions spread across the network. Ukraine has stressed that civilian aircraft are not targets and formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization on Wednesday about growing risks in Russian airspace. The second night of disruption came just two days after Zelensky warned airlines and passengers about those risks. “Russian authorities are not properly informing people about this, Russian airspace will effectively be closing – the war started by Russia is closing its skies,” Zelensky said. Photograph: Geoff Pugh/Shutterstock Jeffrey Archer Jeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86 Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’ Harry Cockburn Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.31 EDT First published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling author and former MP whose political career ended in disgrace when he was imprisoned for perjury, has died at the age of 86. Archer, who was a Conservative MP for five years before serving as the party’s deputy chair, died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home “between writing sessions” on Monday, his publisher HarperCollins said. He had a successful career as an author and was made a life peer in 1992. During a run to become mayor of London for the Conservatives in 1999, his political career was in effect ended when it emerged he had lied in court over a decade earlier when a newspaper accused him of paying money to a sex worker. He was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice and imprisoned for four years. An Old Bailey jury found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Star newspaper in 1987 in which he had been awarded £500,000 in damages. View image in fullscreen Jeffrey Archer with his wife, Mary, arriving at the high court for the eighth day of his libel action against the Star newspaper and its editor, Lloyd Turner. Photograph: PA He was released early in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024. Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK’s chief executive and Archer’s editor, said: “It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer’s editor. “He was the master storyteller and an editor’s dream – phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the team nature of great publishing.” Archer’s death came just one day before the publication of his new novel, Adam and Eve, on Tuesday 6 October. His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, was published in 1976, two years after bankruptcy marked the end of his time as a sitting MP. This marked the beginning of an enviable writing career. Archer spent a total of 14 years and five months on the Sunday Times bestseller lists and over five years on the New York Times bestseller lists, selling 300 million books in 119 countries in 49 languages. His 1979 novel Kane and Abel remains among the best-selling books in the world, having sold more than 30 million copies to date. View image in fullscreen Jeffrey Archer arrives for the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral, London on 16 September 2025. Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImage His death came less than 24 hours after Archer had met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at the Leicester Square Theatre in central London on Sunday, HarperCollins said. Writing on X, Brandreth said: “Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel – he said it was to be his last . “He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last.” Archer was first elected an MP in a 1969 byelection for the constituency of Louth in Lincolnshire when he was 29 years old, having already worked as a Conservative councillor for Havering in north-east London, a period during which he also ran a Mayfair art gallery. Archer cast himself as a centrist in parliament, frequently rebelling against the right wing of the Conservative party, but his political career stalled when he became the victim of a fraudulent investment scheme, which left him almost half a million pounds in debt. He said he would therefore not stand in the 1974 election “due to financial difficulties”. His first novel was a direct effort to regain financial control – a move that paid off, and Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less was adapted for radio, and later, for TV. By the mid-1980s Archer had written several successful novels as well as short stories, plays and children’s books. As his literary career bore fruit, Archer returned to politics, becoming a popular speaker at grassroots events, leading Margaret Thatcher to appoint him deputy chairman of the Conservative party in 1985. But in October 1986 he became embroiled in scandal when the News of the World claimed he’d spent £2,000 to pay off a “vice girl”, a story immediately followed by a more detailed story in the Star alleging Archer had paid a woman named Monica Coghlan for sex. Archer sued the Star, and the case came to court the following year, winning £500,000 in damages but sowing the seeds for his downfall over a decade later. When the allegations broke, the leader of the Conservative party at the time, William Hague, expelled Archer from the party saying: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.” At the time he was charged in 2000, he was also making headlines by starring in his own West End play The Accused, which ran at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in London, and in which Archer’s character played an alleged murderer on trial and in which the audience voted on whether they believed Archer’s character was guilty or innocent at the end of each performance. Archer’s perjury trial began on 30 May 2001, a month after Monica Coghlan was killed in a road traffic accident. Following sentencing he was imprisoned at Belmarsh, a category A prison in London but later moved to four other prisons before his release in 2003, having served half of his sentence. Despite retaining his seat in the House of Lords, Archer did not take an active role in the upper chamber of parliament and gave up his seat in 2024. The former Tory minister, Nadhim Zahawi, paid tribute to Archer, writing on X: “Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey’s company.” Archer had been due to be at the Cheltenham festival later in the month to discuss his forthcoming novel. Archer is survived by his wife, Mary, and their sons, William and James. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/16/fami.text: The families of children killed in a roof collapse at a school in northwest Pakistan called for "justice" on Friday, a day after more than 30 pupils and a teacher were crushed to death.A woman teacher and 34 students, mostly younger than 14, died in the building collapse in the city of Peshawar on Thursday morning."The parents of all these children must receive justice," tailor Muhammad Wahab, who lost his 11-year-old nephew Hammad in the accident, told the AFP news agency on Friday."I appeal to our rulers," he said, adding that Hammad had been "doing well in school" before the tragedy.Dozens of people gathered outside the school on Friday to mourn the children who were killed in the collapse, which officials blamed on dilapidated infrastructure.One grief-stricken father showed AFP a picture on his mobile phone of his young daughter, dressed in red and gold, who lost her life.Another parent, Asadullah, said he lost a son, nephew and three other close relatives in the tragedy."The children were good students and often achieved top positions in their classes," he told AFP. "They happily went to school every day."Residents and rescuers described chaotic scenes in the aftermath of Thursday's collapse, as people scrambled to pull children out from under the rubble.A man named Sohail told AFP that "everyone began screaming in panic" when his niece, who had escaped the building, arrived home to tell them it had collapsed."When I arrived at the scene, I saw around 10 to 15 children trapped beneath the rubble, with debris piled up to their necks. We quickly pulled them out," he said.School owner detainedImages released by emergency services showed rescue workers in high-visibility vests scrambling to move debris, rubble and dirt.A senior official in Peshawar told AFP that initial reports suggested the roof collapse was due to "weak infrastructure"."The school owner has been detained," the official said on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to talk to media.Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed "deep sorrow and grief over the loss of precious lives" in an X post.President Asif Ali Zardari described the roof collapse as a "heartbreaking tragedy".Building collapses are common in Pakistan, largely due to poor safety standards and substandard construction materials in the South Asian nation of more than 240 million people.In June, more than a dozen children were killed when a roof collapsed at a tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore.In 2025, 27 people were killed and 10 injured when a five-storey building collapsed in the impoverished Lyari area of the southern city of Karachi.
